newsitem.title: UK: Dollar to struggle to pierce top of trading ranges.
newsitem.headline: Dollar to struggle to pierce top of trading ranges.

text.p: The dollar's meek peformance in a week of potentially bullish news will prevent it from piercing the top of its seven-week old trading range near 1.50 marks in the near-term, analysts said.
News of U.S. military intervention in Iraq and of Russian President Boris Yeltsin's planned heart operation failed to move the dollar out of its 1.4680-1.4695 mark trading band this week.
Even though the dollar picked up momentum on the back of robust U.S. jobs growth on Friday, it was reined in by solid offers at 1.49 marks and above 109.40 yen, traders said.

"The U.S. data supports the argument for a Fed rate hike this month but probably by only 25 basis points, and the forex market doesn't find this very exciting," said Jonathon Griggs, head of research for treasury products at BZW in London.
The non-farm payroll headline figure, showing a rise of 250,000, was a touch above forecasts for a 244,000 increase.
The real market surprise came from a drop in the jobless rate to 5.1 percent, a seven-year low, from 5.4 percent in July. Jobs growth in July was revised up to 228,000 from 193,000.
U.S. Labor Secretary Robert Reich said there was no sign yet of wage-push inflation despite strong job creation.
"It would have needed a stronger headline figure for the dollar to become more active," said Griggs. "Dollar/mark is not going to make much headway on that figure."

The dollar blipped lower initially after a sharp initial decline in the Treasury market but recovered to session highs around 1.49 marks and 109.36 yen as the market digested the upwards revision to July jobs data and the robust details of the report, dealers said.
At 1505 GMT the dollar traded at 1.4885/95 marks and 109.29/36 yen compared with 1.4850/60 and 109.10/19 in late European trading on Thursday.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said interest rate rise speculation was likely to prevent the dollar from skidding much lower.

"But even if the Fed raises rates by 50 basis points I don't see much upside for the dollar," said Edmonds. "The problem is that the market is poised to get worried about a potential slowdown in the U.S. economy while on the other side of the equation the German economy is picking up speed."
The OECD said on Thursday the German economy will turn up in the second half and recover into 1997. The organisation predicted 0.5 percent growth this year and 2.4 percent in 1997.
A saving grace for the dollar might emerge if the mark stays weak on its European crosses, analysts said.

The mark fell to six-week lows against the lira 1013 per mark and shed further ground against the French franc to trade back down to 3.4140 per mark. A sharp fall in the Swiss franc against the mark also helped the dollar, dealers said.
The key level to watch will be 1.4920 marks where European central banks were rumoured to have sell offers, traders said.
"It's got to be encouraging that the dollar continues to be at the top of the range," said Andrew Chaveriat, analyst at Banque Paribas in London.
"But the market still has to shake off its summer torpor, and there are thought to be a lot of sellers in the 1.4920 to 1.4950 range," said Chaveriat.

The focus next week will be on the remaining data the FOMC will have available when it meets on September 24. These include July consumer credit figures on Monday, the Beige book on U.S. economic conditions on Wednesday, August consumer and producer prices on Thursday and August retail sales on Friday.
Dollar/yen's fortunes are likely to be limited in the near-term by exporter sales offers around 109.40/50, dealers said. -- London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
